stat1-w1-q1.question: Which of these variables is ordinal categorical?
stat1-w1-q1.explanation: T-shirt sizes have a natural order: S < M < L < XL, so it is ordinal. Blood group, city and brand have no 'smaller-bigger' order; they are nominal.

stat1-w1-q2.question: What type of variable is the number of goals scored in a football match?
stat1-w1-q2.explanation: Goals can only be 0, 1, 2, ...; there is no such thing as 2.5 goals. The values are countable, so it is discrete numerical. It would be continuous only if any value in between were possible.

stat1-w1-q3.question: What type of variable is the PIN code of a student's address (e.g. 600036)?
stat1-w1-q3.explanation: A PIN code is just a label for an area. The average or difference of two PIN codes has no meaning, so it is nominal categorical. Trap: seeing digits and treating it as discrete numerical.

stat1-w1-q4.question: Which of these variables is on an interval scale (no true zero)?
stat1-w1-q4.explanation: 0°C does not mean 'no temperature'; it is just a reference point, so °C is an interval scale. For weight, income and number of books, 0 really means 'nothing', so they are ratio scales.

stat1-w1-q5.question: A dataset has 250 students. For each student, name, age, state and the marks in three subjects (Maths, Stats, English) are recorded in separate columns. How many cases and how many variables does this dataset have?
stat1-w1-q5.explanation: Each student is one row (case), so 250 cases. Columns: name, age, state, Maths, Stats, English = 6 variables. Trap: counting 'marks' as a single variable, when the three subjects are three separate columns.

stat1-w1-q6.question: Which of these statements is correct?
options: The mean of ordinal data is always meaningful
40 kg is double 20 kg, because weight is on a ratio scale
The player with jersey number 10 is twice as good as the one with jersey 5
stat1-w1-q6.explanation: Weight has a true zero, so stating a ratio ('double') is valid. °C is an interval scale, so the ratio is wrong; a jersey number is only a label; and the gaps between ordinal categories are not equal, so their mean is not always meaningful.

stat1-w1-q7.question: The revenue of a company was recorded every year from 2015 to 2024. What type of data is this?
stat1-w1-q7.explanation: The same thing (the company's revenue) is recorded again and again over time (every year), so this is time series data. It would be cross-sectional if the revenue of many companies were recorded for a single year. Nominal and ordinal are types of categorical variables, and revenue is numerical.

stat1-w1-q8.question: Which of these variables is nominal categorical?
options: State code on a vehicle number plate (MH, DL, KA)
stat1-w1-q8.explanation: A state code is just a label; MH, DL and KA have no 'smaller-bigger' order, so it is nominal. Rank, star rating and education level have a natural order, so they are ordinal categorical. Trap: treating rank or rating as nominal, when they clearly have an order.

stat1-w1-q9.question: In a table, each row is a train journey, and the columns are: train number, distance (km), delay (minutes) and class. What is one case in this dataset?
options: The pair of distance and delay
stat1-w1-q9.explanation: Row = case, column = variable. Each row is a train journey, so one case is one train journey. The train number column is a variable, and distance and delay are just two variables, not a case.

stat1-w1-q10.question: A survey asked: 'How many hours do you study per day?' and the answers were recorded only as one of these group labels: '0–1', '1–2', '2–4', '4+' hours. As recorded in the dataset, what type of variable is this?
stat1-w1-q10.explanation: Study time is really continuous, but here only the group (range) is recorded. The groups have an order (0–1 < 1–2 < 2–4 < 4+), but the exact value is unknown and the groups are not even of equal width, so the recorded variable is ordinal categorical; labels like '2–4' and '4+' cannot be averaged. Trap: saying continuous by looking at the underlying quantity; the type depends on the form in which the data is recorded.

stat1-w1-q11.question: In the dataset of an online store, each row is an order. Columns: order ID, number of items, delivery rating (1–5 stars) and payment mode (UPI/card/cash). Which of these variables is discrete numerical?
stat1-w1-q11.explanation: The number of items takes countable values like 1, 2, 3, ... and its average is meaningful, so it is discrete numerical. Order ID is just a label (nominal), the rating has an order but unequal gaps (ordinal), and payment mode is nominal. Trap: seeing the numbers 1–5 in the rating and treating it as discrete numerical.

stat1-w1-q12.question: A hospital dataset has the columns: Patient ID, Age (years), Blood group, Pain level (mild/moderate/severe), Body temperature (°C), Number of visits, Ward number. How many of these variables are categorical?
stat1-w1-q12.explanation: Categorical: Patient ID (label), Blood group (nominal), Pain level (ordinal) and Ward number (label) = 4. Numerical: Age, Body temperature and Number of visits = 3. Trap 2: counting Patient ID and Ward number as numerical because they look like numbers. Trap 5: treating temperature as categorical because °C is an interval scale; an interval scale is still numerical.

stat1-w1-q13.question: Which of these classifications is fully correct (in both parts)?
options: Aadhaar number: discrete numerical; Height: continuous numerical
Year of birth: ratio scale; Weight: ratio scale
Income bracket (low/middle/high): ordinal; Number of children: discrete numerical
Temperature (°C): ratio scale; Blood group: nominal
stat1-w1-q13.explanation: Income bracket has an order (low < middle < high), so it is ordinal, and the number of children is countable, so it is discrete numerical: both parts are correct. An Aadhaar number is just a label (nominal), year of birth has an arbitrary zero (interval, not ratio), and °C is also an interval scale. Each wrong option has one correct part, so both parts must be checked.

stat1-w1-q14.question: In Dataset 1, the max temperature and rainfall of 50 Indian cities were recorded on 30 June 2024. In Dataset 2, only Chennai's max temperature was recorded for every day of 2024 (366 days). Which statement is correct?
options: Dataset 1 is cross-sectional (50 cases), Dataset 2 is time series (366 cases)
Dataset 1 is time series (50 cases), Dataset 2 is cross-sectional (366 cases)
Both are time series, because both record a date
Dataset 1 is cross-sectional (1 case), Dataset 2 is time series (1 case)
stat1-w1-q14.explanation: Dataset 1 has many cases (50 cities) at a single time (one day), so it is cross-sectional, and each city is one row = 50 cases. In Dataset 2 the same thing (Chennai) is recorded again and again over time, so it is time series, and each day is one row = 366 cases. Trap: calling both time series just because of the date, or treating Chennai as a single case and counting the 366 rows as 1 case.

stat1-w1-q15.question: The values of a variable can be ordered and the difference of two values is meaningful, but saying 'this value is double that value' is not meaningful. On which scale is this variable, and which example fits?
stat1-w1-q15.explanation: Order + meaningful difference, but no true zero (so ratios are wrong): this is the mark of an interval scale. For calendar years, 2020 − 2010 = 10 years is meaningful, but year 0 is not 'the start of time', so calling 2020 double of 1010 is meaningless. For ordinal data differences are not meaningful, and salary is a ratio scale because ₹0 is a true zero.

stat1-w2-q1.question: Which is the most appropriate measure of center for a nominal categorical variable (like favourite colour)?
stat1-w2-q1.explanation: Nominal categories allow neither arithmetic nor ordering, so the mean and median cannot be computed. Only the mode (the most frequent category) works. Standard deviation is a measure of spread, not center.

stat1-w2-q2.question: In a survey of 50 people, 15 named tea as their favourite drink. What is the relative frequency of tea?
stat1-w2-q2.explanation: Relative frequency = 15 / 50 = 0.30. Option 15 is just the frequency, and 0.15 would come from mistakenly dividing by 100.

stat1-w2-q3.question: Out of 200 students, 50 chose the Science stream. What will be the angle of the Science slice in a pie chart?
stat1-w2-q3.explanation: Angle = (50 / 200) × 360° = 0.25 × 360° = 90°. Trap: writing 25% directly as 25°, or taking the frequency 50 itself as the degrees.

stat1-w2-q4.question: Ratings from 9 customers: Poor 2, Average 3, Good 3, Excellent 1. What is the median category of this ordinal data?
stat1-w2-q4.explanation: n = 9, so the median is at the 5th position. Cumulative count in order: Poor = positions 1-2, Average = 3-5, Good = 6-8, Excellent = 9. The 5th position falls in Average. Trap: taking Good as the median because its frequency is also 3, but the median comes from position, not frequency.

stat1-w2-q5.question: In what order are the bars arranged in a Pareto chart?
options: Alphabetical order of the category names
Descending frequency, along with a cumulative % line
stat1-w2-q5.explanation: The purpose of a Pareto chart is to show which few categories account for the largest share, so the bars go from largest to smallest with a cumulative % line alongside. Ascending order is the opposite.

stat1-w2-q6.question: In a bar chart, Brand A's sales are 92 and Brand B's are 96, but the y-axis starts at 90 instead of 0. How many times longer will B's bar look compared to A's bar in the graph?
stat1-w2-q6.explanation: The axis starts at 90, so the visible heights are 92 − 90 = 2 and 96 − 90 = 6, which means B's bar will look 6 / 2 = 3 times longer. The actual ratio is only 96 / 92 ≈ 1.04. This is why a truncated axis is misleading.

stat1-w2-q7.question: In a pie chart, one slice has an angle of 54°. What percent of the total is this category?
stat1-w2-q7.explanation: Percent = (angle / 360°) × 100 = (54 / 360) × 100 = 15%. Trap 54%: taking the degrees directly as a percent. 30% would come from dividing by 180° instead of 360°.

stat1-w2-q8.question: Favourite fruit in a survey: Mango 14, Apple 9, Banana 14, Grapes 6. What is the mode of this data?
stat1-w2-q8.explanation: Mango and Banana both have frequency 14, the highest, so the data is bimodal and both are modes. Trap Mango: stopping at the first highest frequency. Trap 14: writing the frequency as the mode; the mode is a category, not its count.

stat1-w2-q9.question: In a frequency table, the relative frequencies of 4 categories are 0.35, 0.25, 0.15 and x. What is the value of x?
stat1-w2-q9.explanation: All relative frequencies add up to 1: x = 1 − (0.35 + 0.25 + 0.15) = 1 − 0.75 = 0.25. Trap 0.75: writing the sum of the other three and forgetting to subtract it from 1.

stat1-w2-q10.question: In a survey, 250 people were asked their mode of travel. In the pie chart, 'Bus' has an angle of 72°. How many people chose Bus?
stat1-w2-q10.explanation: Relative frequency = 72 / 360 = 0.2, so frequency = 0.2 × 250 = 50. Trap 72: taking the angle as the count. Trap 180: reading 72° as 72% and computing 0.72 × 250. 20 is only the percent, not the number of people.

stat1-w2-q11.question: A shop's 80 complaints: Billing 8, Late delivery 36, Other 4, Wrong item 12, Damaged item 20. In the Pareto chart, what is the cumulative % line after the first 2 bars?
stat1-w2-q11.explanation: In a Pareto chart the bars go in descending order: Late delivery 36, Damaged item 20, Wrong item 12, Billing 8, Other 4. First 2 bars = 36 + 20 = 56, cumulative % = 56 / 80 = 70%. Trap 55%: taking the first two in the order listed (8 + 36 = 44, and 44 / 80 = 55%). Trap 56%: taking the count as the percent.

stat1-w2-q12.question: 45% of the 200 students of College A and 30% of the 400 students of College B have Cricket as their favourite sport. In a pie chart made for both colleges together (600 students), what will be the angle for Cricket?
stat1-w2-q12.explanation: Cricket students: 0.45 × 200 = 90 in A and 0.30 × 400 = 120 in B, total 210. Relative frequency = 210 / 600 = 0.35, angle = 0.35 × 360° = 126°. Trap 135°: taking the simple average of the two percentages (37.5%), although the colleges have different sizes. Trap 270°: adding the separate angles of the two colleges (162° + 108°). Trap 35°: taking the percent as degrees.

stat1-w2-q13.question: A pie chart has 4 categories: A has an angle of 150°, B 90°, C 75° and D the rest. The frequency of D is 30. What is the frequency of A?
stat1-w2-q13.explanation: Angle of D = 360 − (150 + 90 + 75) = 45°. 45° ↔ 30 people, so total = 30 × 360 / 45 = 240. Frequency of A = (150 / 360) × 240 = 100. Trap 150: taking the angle as the frequency. 240 is the total, not A, and 60 is the frequency of B.

stat1-w2-q14.question: Ratings of 20 customers (Poor < Average < Good < Excellent): Poor 7, Average 4, Good 6, Excellent 3. Which of these statements is correct?
options: The mode is Poor and the median is Average
The mode is Poor and the median is Good
Both the mode and the median are Poor
The median is Average and the relative frequency of 'Good or above' is 0.30
stat1-w2-q14.explanation: Mode = highest frequency = Poor (7). n = 20, so the median is at positions 10th and 11th. Cumulative: Poor 1–7, Average 8–11, Good 12–17, Excellent 18–20, so both positions are in Average: median = Average. 'Good or above' = (6 + 3) / 20 = 0.45, not 0.30. Trap: assuming the mode and median are the same; the median comes from the position, not from the frequency.

stat1-w2-q15.question: In a graph, Brand A's sales are 50 and Brand B's are 100. The designer made B's bar 2 times as tall as A's bar and also 2 times as wide. In reality, B's sales are how many times A's sales, and how many times bigger does B's bar (by area) look than A's?
stat1-w2-q15.explanation: Real ratio = 100 / 50 = 2. Bar area = height × width, so the visible ratio = 2 × 2 = 4. The eye judges area, so the difference looks 4 times instead of double. This is why all bars in a bar chart have the same width. Trap 'looks 2 times': looking only at the height and ignoring the change in width.

stat1-w3-q1.question: What is the mean of the data 2, 5, 6, 9, 13?
stat1-w3-q1.explanation: Sum = 2 + 5 + 6 + 9 + 13 = 35, n = 5, mean = 35 / 5 = 7. Option 6 is the median (the middle value), and 35 is just the sum.

stat1-w3-q2.question: What is the median of the data 12, 5, 9, 20, 7, 15?
stat1-w3-q2.explanation: Sort it: 5, 7, 9, 12, 15, 20. n = 6 is even, so median = (9 + 12) / 2 = 10.5. Option 11.33 is the mean (68 / 6), and 9 or 12 alone are the middle values, not the median.

stat1-w3-q3.question: A dataset has mean 20 and standard deviation 4. Each value is multiplied by 3 and then 2 is added. What will the new mean and new SD be?
stat1-w3-q3.explanation: New mean = 3 × 20 + 2 = 62. Adding has no effect on the SD, only multiplying does: 3 × 4 = 12. Trap: adding 2 to the SD as well (14), or applying the variance's a² factor to the SD (4 × 9 = 36).

stat1-w3-q4.question: Treat the data 1, 3, 5, 7 as the whole population. What is the population variance?
stat1-w3-q4.explanation: Mean = 16 / 4 = 4. Deviations −3, −1, 1, 3; squares 9, 1, 1, 9; sum = 20. Population variance = 20 / 4 = 5. Option 6.67 is the sample variance (20 / 3), and 2.24 is the standard deviation, not the variance.

stat1-w3-q5.question: A dataset has Q1 = 20 and Q3 = 35. According to the 1.5 × IQR rule, which of these values is an outlier?
stat1-w3-q5.explanation: IQR = 35 − 20 = 15. Upper fence = 35 + 1.5 × 15 = 57.5. Only 60 is above this fence, so it is the outlier. 57 is very close to the fence but less than 57.5, so it is not an outlier.

stat1-w3-q6.question: The mean of 10 numbers came out as 15. Later it was found that a value 24 had been wrongly written as 42. What is the correct mean?
stat1-w3-q6.explanation: Wrong sum = 15 × 10 = 150. Correct sum = 150 − 42 + 24 = 132. Correct mean = 132 / 10 = 13.2. Trap 16.8: applying the correction in the opposite direction (150 + 18 = 168).

stat1-w3-q7.question: What is the mode of the data 3, 7, 7, 2, 9, 3, 5?
stat1-w3-q7.explanation: 3 and 7 both appear twice and every other value once, so the data is bimodal: the modes are 3 and 7. Trap 7: stopping at the first repeated value. 5 is the median (sorted: 2, 3, 3, 5, 7, 7, 9), not the mode.

stat1-w3-q8.question: What is the range of the data 14, 9, 22, 5, 17?
stat1-w3-q8.explanation: Range = max − min = 22 − 5 = 17. Trap 22: writing only the max. 13.4 is the mean (67 / 5), and 3 is the difference between the first and last values (17 − 14), not the range.

stat1-w3-q9.question: For some data, Q1 = 18, median = 25 and Q3 = 31. What is the IQR?
stat1-w3-q9.explanation: IQR = Q3 − Q1 = 31 − 18 = 13. Trap 7: taking median − Q1; trap 6: taking Q3 − median. 24.5 is just the average of Q1 and Q3.

stat1-w3-q10.question: What is the sample variance of the sample data 3, 7, 8, 10, 12?
stat1-w3-q10.explanation: Mean = 40 / 5 = 8. Deviations −5, −1, 0, 2, 4; squares 25, 1, 0, 4, 16; sum = 46. Sample variance = 46 / (5 − 1) = 11.5. Trap 9.2: dividing by n = 5 (the population formula). 3.39 is the sample SD (√11.5), not the variance.

stat1-w3-q11.question: Salaries of 5 employees (in ₹ thousand): 20, 22, 25, 28, 30. A new employee joins at a salary of ₹205 thousand. By how much do the mean and the median increase?
options: Mean up by 30, median up by 1.5
Mean up by 180, median up by 3
stat1-w3-q11.explanation: Before: mean = 125 / 5 = 25, median = 25. After: sum = 330, n = 6, mean = 55; the median of the sorted 20, 22, 25, 28, 30, 205 is (25 + 28) / 2 = 26.5. The mean rises by 30, the median by only 1.5. An outlier pulls the mean a lot and the median only a little. Trap 'median unchanged': with n even, the median becomes the average of the two middle values.

stat1-w3-q12.question: The combined mean of 50 students is 66. Of these, the 30 students of Section A have a mean of 62. What is the mean of the remaining 20 students of Section B?
stat1-w3-q12.explanation: Total sum = 50 × 66 = 3300. Sum of Section A = 30 × 62 = 1860. Sum of Section B = 3300 − 1860 = 1440, mean = 1440 / 20 = 72. Trap 70: assuming the combined mean is the simple average of the two means (66 = (62 + 70) / 2); that only happens when both sections have the same size. Trap 48: dividing 1440 by the wrong group size 30. 1440 is only the sum.

stat1-w3-q13.question: The five-number summary of some data: min = 12, Q1 = 30, median = 38, Q3 = 46, max = 75. Using the 1.5 × IQR rule, which conclusion is correct?
options: At least one outlier, only on the upper side
At least one outlier, only on the lower side
There are outliers on both sides
stat1-w3-q13.explanation: IQR = 46 − 30 = 16, and 1.5 × IQR = 24. Lower fence = 30 − 24 = 6, upper fence = 46 + 24 = 70. Min 12 > 6, so there is no outlier at the bottom; max 75 > 70, so there is at least one outlier at the top. Trap: calling 12 an outlier too because it looks 'far' from the median; it must be compared with the fence.

stat1-w3-q14.question: 10 values have mean 20 and population variance 16. A new value 20 is added to the data. What is the new population variance?
stat1-w3-q14.explanation: Σ(x − μ)² = 10 × 16 = 160. The new value equals the mean, so the mean stays 20 and its deviation is 0, so the sum of squared deviations also stays 160. New variance = 160 / 11 ≈ 14.55. Trap 16: thinking the variance will not change; with a larger n the same sum is divided by a bigger number. Trap 17.6: multiplying 16 by 11 / 10 instead of dividing by 11. 3.81 is the new SD (√14.55), not the variance.

stat1-w3-q15.question: The mean of 5 values is 10. 4 of these values are 6, 9, 11 and 14. What is the population variance of the full data?
stat1-w3-q15.explanation: Total = 5 × 10 = 50, so the 5th value = 50 − (6 + 9 + 11 + 14) = 50 − 40 = 10. Deviations −4, −1, 1, 4, 0; squares 16, 1, 1, 16, 0; sum = 34. Population variance = 34 / 5 = 6.8. Trap 8.5: dividing by n − 1 = 4 (sample variance). 34 is only the sum of squares, and 2.61 is the SD (√6.8).

stat1-w4-q1.question: The correlation between two variables is r = −0.9. What is the most accurate interpretation?
stat1-w4-q1.explanation: The negative sign tells us that when one increases the other decreases, and |r| = 0.9 is close to 1, meaning the relation is strong and linear. It is important to read the sign and the magnitude separately.

stat1-w4-q2.question: Which of these values can the correlation coefficient r never take?
stat1-w4-q2.explanation: r always lies between −1 and 1. 1.3 is outside this range, so it is impossible. 0 and −1 are perfectly valid values.

stat1-w4-q3.question: A table of 100 students: in the hostel, Pass 45, Fail 15. Among day scholars, Pass 25, Fail 15. What is the proportion of hostel students who passed?
stat1-w4-q3.explanation: Hostel row total = 45 + 15 = 60. Proportion = 45 / 60 = 0.75. Trap: 45 / 100 = 0.45 is the joint proportion, 70 / 100 = 0.70 is the overall pass rate, and 25 / 40 = 0.625 is for day scholars.

stat1-w4-q4.question: The covariance of two variables is 12, the SD of x is 3 and the SD of y is 5 (all computed with the same divisor). What is the correlation r?
stat1-w4-q4.explanation: r = Cov / (σx σy) = 12 / (3 × 5) = 12 / 15 = 0.8. Option 12 is just the covariance, and 4 = 12 / 3 (dividing by only one SD).

stat1-w4-q5.question: The correlation r between height (x) and weight (y) was computed. Now all heights are converted from cm to inches (divided by 2.54), keeping weight the same. What will the new r be?
options: The sign of r will flip
stat1-w4-q5.explanation: r is unit-free. Multiplying or dividing by a positive constant changes both the covariance and the SD by the same factor, which cancels out. The sign would flip only if we multiplied by a negative constant.

stat1-w4-q6.question: x: 2, 4, 6, 8 and y: 3, 7, 5, 9. What is the correlation coefficient r?
stat1-w4-q6.explanation: x̄ = 5, ȳ = 6. Deviations x: −3, −1, 1, 3; y: −3, 1, −1, 3. Sum of products = 9 − 1 − 1 + 9 = 16. Σdx² = 20, Σdy² = 20. r = 16 / √(20 × 20) = 16 / 20 = 0.8. Trap: 4 is the population covariance (16 / 4), and 0.64 = r².

stat1-w4-q7.question: The covariance of two numerical variables is −15. What does this tell us?
options: The relation is strong, because |−15| is a big number
When one variable increases, the other generally decreases
There is no relation between the two variables
stat1-w4-q7.explanation: The sign of the covariance gives the direction: negative means that when one increases the other generally decreases. The value of the covariance depends on the units, so the strength cannot be judged from −15 alone; for strength we need the correlation r. Trap: reading a big covariance number as a strong relation.

stat1-w4-q8.question: Across the districts of a state, districts with more hospitals record more deaths per year (r = 0.8). Which of these is the most correct conclusion?
options: A third variable such as the district's population can increase both
r = 0.8 means that 80% of deaths are caused by hospitals
stat1-w4-q8.explanation: Correlation does not prove causation. Bigger districts have more people, so they have more hospitals and also more deaths; population drives both. r = 0.8 is only the strength of the linear relation, not a percentage.

stat1-w4-q9.question: Two-way table of 100 people: Male: Yes 30, No 20; Female: Yes 40, No 10. What proportion of all the people are both 'Female and Yes'?
stat1-w4-q9.explanation: This is a joint proportion, so divide by the grand total: 40 / 100 = 0.4. Trap 0.8: 40 / 50 is the conditional proportion within the Female row. 0.57 ≈ 40 / 70 is the conditional proportion within the Yes column, and 0.7 is the overall Yes proportion.

stat1-w4-q10.question: x: 1, 2, 3, 4 and y: 10, 8, 6, 4. What is the population covariance Cov(x, y)?
stat1-w4-q10.explanation: x̄ = 2.5, ȳ = 7. Deviations of x: −1.5, −0.5, 0.5, 1.5; of y: 3, 1, −1, −3. Products: −4.5, −0.5, −0.5, −4.5, sum = −10. Population covariance = −10 / 4 = −2.5. Trap −10: forgetting to divide by n. −3.33 is the sample covariance (−10 / 3). The sign is negative because y falls as x rises.

stat1-w4-q11.question: In a factory, 36 of the 60 morning-shift workers drink tea, and 24 of the 40 night-shift workers do. What is correct to say about the association between shift and drinking tea?
options: More morning-shift workers drink tea (36 > 24), so there is an association
The proportion of tea drinkers is higher in the night shift
The correlation r must be computed to check the association
The proportion is 0.6 in both shifts, so no association is seen
stat1-w4-q11.explanation: Compare conditional proportions: morning 36 / 60 = 0.6, night 24 / 40 = 0.6. They are equal, so changing the shift does not change the proportion of tea drinkers: no association. Trap: comparing raw counts (36 vs 24), although the two shifts have different sizes. The correlation r is for numerical variables; here both variables are categorical.

stat1-w4-q12.question: For x and y, Cov(x, y) = 8 and r = 0.4. New variables u = 3x + 2 and v = −2y + 5 are made. What are Cov(u, v) and r(u, v)?
stat1-w4-q12.explanation: The shifts (+2, +5) have no effect on the covariance. The scaling does: Cov(u, v) = 3 × (−2) × 8 = −48. The magnitude of r stays the same, but one factor is negative, so the sign flips: r(u, v) = −0.4. Trap 'r 0.4': treating r as unit-free and keeping the sign too. Trap −16: using only the factor −2 and forgetting the 3.

stat1-w4-q13.question: A school has 200 students: 120 boys and 80 girls. The pass rate of boys is 0.75 and the pass rate of the whole school is 0.72. What is the pass rate of girls?
stat1-w4-q13.explanation: Total passed = 0.72 × 200 = 144. Boys passed = 0.75 × 120 = 90. Girls passed = 144 − 90 = 54, so the pass rate of girls = 54 / 80 = 0.675. Trap 0.69: assuming 0.72 is the simple average of the two rates. 0.27 = 54 / 200 is a joint proportion, and 0.375 = 54 / 144 is 'the share of girls among those who passed'.

stat1-w4-q14.question: x: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2 and y = x², i.e. y: 4, 1, 0, 1, 4. What is the correlation r, and what does it correctly mean?
options: r = 0, but y has a perfect non-linear relation with x
r = 0, so x and y have no relation
r = 1, because y is fully determined by x
stat1-w4-q14.explanation: x̄ = 0, ȳ = 2. Deviations of x: −2, −1, 0, 1, 2; of y: 2, −1, −2, −1, 2. Products: −4, 1, 0, −1, 4, sum = 0, so r = 0. But y = x² is an exact U-shaped relation. r measures only linear relation, so saying 'no relation' is wrong. Trap r = 1: mistaking 'y depends fully on x' for a perfect linear relation.

stat1-w4-q15.question: In a course, Online students: Pass 48, Fail 32; Offline students: Pass 54, Fail 18. Which of these statements is correct?
options: Of the 102 students who passed, 48 were online, so the online pass rate is about 0.47
Both groups have the same pass rate, so there is no association
0.36 of the students who failed were online
The online pass rate is 0.60 and the offline rate is 0.75, so mode and result are associated
stat1-w4-q15.explanation: Row-wise conditional proportions: online 48 / 80 = 0.60, offline 54 / 72 = 0.75. The rates differ, so mode and result are associated. 48 / 102 ≈ 0.47 is 'the share of online students among those who passed', not the online pass rate (the condition is reversed). Of the 50 students who failed, 32 / 50 = 0.64 were online, not 0.36.

stat1-w5-q1.question: A student has 3 shirts and 4 pants. How many different outfits of one shirt and one pant can be made?
stat1-w5-q1.explanation: First choose a shirt (3 ways), then a pant (4 ways). By the multiplication rule, 3 × 4 = 12. Trap: the addition rule 3 + 4 = 7 applies only when you choose just one item.

stat1-w5-q2.question: What is the value of 5C2?
stat1-w5-q2.explanation: 5C2 = 5! / (2! × 3!) = 120 / (2 × 6) = 10. Option 20 = 5P2, where order counts; for a combination we divide it by 2!.

stat1-w5-q3.question: In how many ways can 6 friends sit around a round table (arrangements that differ only by rotation are considered the same)?
stat1-w5-q3.explanation: Circular arrangement = (6 − 1)! = 5! = 120. 720 = 6! is the answer for a line, counting rotations separately. 360 would come if clockwise and anticlockwise were also treated as the same (like a necklace), which is not stated here.

stat1-w5-q4.question: In how many different ways can the letters of the word 'BANANA' be arranged?
stat1-w5-q4.explanation: 6 letters: A three times, N twice, B once. Arrangements = 6! / (3! × 2!) = 720 / 12 = 60. Trap: dividing only by 3! (120) or only by 2! (360); you must account for both repeated letters.

stat1-w5-q5.question: In a 4-digit PIN, each digit can be anything from 0 to 9 and digits can repeat. How many different PINs are possible?
stat1-w5-q5.explanation: 10 choices at each position, 4 positions: 10 × 10 × 10 × 10 = 10⁴ = 10000. 5040 = 10P4 would apply if repetition were not allowed.

stat1-w5-q6.question: A committee of 4 people is to be formed from 5 men and 4 women, with at least 1 woman. In how many ways can this be done?
stat1-w5-q6.explanation: Total committees = 9C4 = 126. Without any woman (only men) = 5C4 = 5. At least one woman = 126 − 5 = 121. Trap 224: first fixing one woman (4 ways) and choosing the other 3 from any of the 8 (8C3 = 56), 4 × 56 = 224, which counts the same committee several times.

stat1-w5-q7.question: A race has 8 runners. In how many ways can the Gold, Silver and Bronze medals be awarded?
stat1-w5-q7.explanation: The medals are different, so order matters: 8P3 = 8 × 7 × 6 = 336. Trap 56: 8C3 only picks the 3 winners, not their order. Trap 512: 8³, as if one runner could win more than one medal.

stat1-w5-q8.question: In how many ways can 5 different books be arranged in a row on a shelf?
stat1-w5-q8.explanation: n different things can be arranged in a row in n! ways: 5! = 5 × 4 × 3 × 2 × 1 = 120. Trap 24: (5 − 1)! is the formula for a circular arrangement, not a row. Trap 25: 5 × 5, as if one book could go in two places.

stat1-w5-q9.question: A canteen has 4 veg and 3 non-veg dishes. A student will take only one dish. How many choices does the student have?
stat1-w5-q9.explanation: Only one dish is taken, either veg or non-veg (not both), so by the addition rule: 4 + 3 = 7. Trap 12: the multiplication rule (4 × 3) would apply if one veg and one non-veg dish were both taken. 2 is just the number of types of dish.

stat1-w5-q10.question: A team of 4 is to be chosen from 10 students, and Riya must be in it. How many ways are there?
stat1-w5-q10.explanation: Riya is fixed, so 3 more are chosen from the other 9 students: 9C3 = 84. Trap 210: 10C4, ignoring the condition about Riya. Trap 126: 9C4, these are the teams without Riya. Trap 36: 9C2, choosing only 2 more people after Riya.

stat1-w5-q11.question: 3-digit numbers are formed from the digits 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 (no digit repeated). How many of these numbers are even?
stat1-w5-q11.explanation: For an even number the last digit is 2 or 4 (2 ways). Then, from the remaining 4 digits, the first position has 4 ways and the middle 3: 2 × 4 × 3 = 24. Trap 60: 5P3, all the 3-digit numbers. Trap 36: this is the count of odd numbers (3 × 4 × 3).

stat1-w5-q12.question: 6 people are to sit in a row, and 2 particular friends always sit together (next to each other). How many arrangements are possible?
stat1-w5-q12.explanation: Treat the two friends as one block: now there are 5 units, with 5! = 120 arrangements. Inside the block the two friends can sit in 2! = 2 ways. Total = 120 × 2 = 240. Trap 120: forgetting the 2! inside the block. Trap 480: this is 720 − 240, i.e. when the friends do not sit together.

stat1-w5-q13.question: A committee of 5 is to be formed from 7 boys and 5 girls with exactly 2 girls, and a particular boy, Aman, must not be on the committee. How many ways are there?
stat1-w5-q13.explanation: Girls: 5C2 = 10. Boys: 3 are needed, from the 6 boys other than Aman: 6C3 = 20. Total = 10 × 20 = 200. Trap 350: forgetting the condition on Aman and using 7C3 = 35. Trap 150: using 6C2 = 15 for the boys, when 5 − 2 = 3 boys are needed. Trap 792: 12C5, ignoring all the conditions.

stat1-w5-q14.question: 5 boys and 5 girls sit around a round table so that boys and girls alternate (girls on both sides of every boy). How many arrangements are possible (arrangements that are rotations of each other count as the same)?
stat1-w5-q14.explanation: First seat the 5 boys around the table: (5 − 1)! = 4! = 24 ways. Now the boys form 5 gaps that are distinct from each other, so the 5 girls can sit in them in 5! = 120 ways. Total = 24 × 120 = 2880. Trap 14400: using 5! for the boys too, i.e. counting rotations as different. Trap 362880: 9!, ignoring the alternating condition.

stat1-w5-q15.question: In how many arrangements of the letters of the word 'ARRANGE' do the two R's come together (next to each other)?
stat1-w5-q15.explanation: ARRANGE has 7 letters: A twice, R twice, and N, G, E. Treat the two R's as one block 'RR': units = RR, A, A, N, G, E = 6, with A appearing twice. Arrangements = 6! / 2! = 720 / 2 = 360. The two R's in the block are identical, so we do not multiply by 2!. Trap 720: forgetting that A repeats. Trap 1260: 7! / (2! × 2!), all arrangements without the condition.

stat1-w6-q1.question: A coin is tossed 3 times. How many outcomes are in the sample space?
stat1-w6-q1.explanation: Each toss has 2 outcomes, 3 tosses: 2 × 2 × 2 = 2³ = 8 (HHH, HHT, ..., TTT). Trap: doing 3 × 2 = 6, which is applying the multiplication rule incorrectly.

stat1-w6-q2.question: P(A) = 0.35. What is P(A') (the complement of A)?
stat1-w6-q2.explanation: P(A') = 1 − P(A) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65. 1.35 cannot be a probability because it is greater than 1.

stat1-w6-q3.question: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.4 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. What is P(A ∪ B)?
stat1-w6-q3.explanation: P(A ∪ B) = 0.5 + 0.4 − 0.2 = 0.7. Trap: forgetting to subtract the intersection and writing 0.9; the common part gets counted twice.

stat1-w6-q4.question: Two fair dice are thrown. What is the probability that the sum of the two numbers is 8?
stat1-w6-q4.explanation: Ordered outcomes with sum 8: (2,6), (3,5), (4,4), (5,3), (6,2) = 5. P = 5 / 36. Trap 5/11: treating the possible sums (2 to 12) as 11 equally likely outcomes, which is wrong.

stat1-w6-q5.question: A card is drawn from a deck of 52 cards. What is the probability that the card is a king or a heart?
stat1-w6-q5.explanation: P(king) = 4/52, P(heart) = 13/52, P(king of hearts) = 1/52. P = 4/52 + 13/52 − 1/52 = 16/52 = 4/13. Trap 17/52: counting the king of hearts twice.

stat1-w6-q6.question: A bag has 5 red and 3 blue balls. 2 balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both balls are the same colour?
stat1-w6-q6.explanation: Total ways = 8C2 = 28. Both red = 5C2 = 10, both blue = 3C2 = 3. P = (10 + 3) / 28 = 13/28. Traps: 15/28 is the probability of different colours (5 × 3), 5/14 = 10/28 is just both red, and 17/32 is the with-replacement answer (25 + 9) / 64.

stat1-w6-q7.question: A bag has 3 red, 5 green and 2 yellow balls. One ball is drawn at random. What is the probability that it is green?
stat1-w6-q7.explanation: Total balls = 3 + 5 + 2 = 10, green = 5, so P = 5/10 = 1/2. Trap 1/3: treating the three colours as equally likely outcomes; the equally likely outcomes are the balls, not the colours. Trap 5/8: comparing green only with red + green (8). 1/5 is the probability of yellow.

stat1-w6-q8.question: A and B are mutually exclusive events, P(A) = 0.3 and P(B) = 0.45. What is P(A ∪ B)?
stat1-w6-q8.explanation: Mutually exclusive means P(A ∩ B) = 0, so P(A ∪ B) = 0.3 + 0.45 = 0.75. Trap 0.135: computing P(A) × P(B), which is the intersection formula for independent events. Trap 0.615: treating the events as independent and taking 0.75 − 0.135.

stat1-w6-q9.question: A fair die is rolled. Event A = 'getting a prime number'. Which outcomes are in event A?
stat1-w6-q9.explanation: Among the outcomes 1 to 6, the prime numbers are 2, 3 and 5, so A = {2, 3, 5}. Trap: treating 1 as prime (1 is not prime), or forgetting 2 because it is even. {2, 4, 6} is the 'even number' event.

stat1-w6-q10.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the difference of the two numbers (larger − smaller) is exactly 2?
stat1-w6-q10.explanation: Ordered outcomes: (1,3), (3,1), (2,4), (4,2), (3,5), (5,3), (4,6), (6,4) = 8. P = 8/36 = 2/9. Trap 1/9: counting only (1,3), (2,4), (3,5), (4,6) and forgetting the reverse order (4/36). Trap 4/21: treating the 21 unordered pairs as equally likely. 1/6 is the probability of a double (difference 0).

stat1-w6-q11.question: P(A) = 0.6, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∪ B) = 0.8. What is the probability that exactly one of the events A and B occurs?
stat1-w6-q11.explanation: First the intersection: P(A ∩ B) = 0.6 + 0.5 − 0.8 = 0.3. Exactly one = union − both = 0.8 − 0.3 = 0.5. Trap 0.3: this is the intersection (both events). Trap 0.8: the union also includes the 'both' part. 1.1 cannot be a probability.

stat1-w6-q12.question: A fair coin is tossed 4 times. What is the probability of getting at least one head and at least one tail?
stat1-w6-q12.explanation: Total outcomes = 2⁴ = 16. Complement: all heads (HHHH) or all tails (TTTT) = 2 outcomes. P = 1 − 2/16 = 14/16 = 7/8. Trap 15/16: finding only 'at least one head' (removing just TTTT) and forgetting HHHH. Trap 3/8: this is the probability of exactly 2 heads (6/16).

stat1-w6-q13.question: One number is chosen at random from the integers 1 to 100. What is the probability that it is divisible by 4 or by 6?
stat1-w6-q13.explanation: Divisible by 4: 25 numbers (4, 8, ..., 100). Divisible by 6: 16 numbers (6, 12, ..., 96). Divisible by both means by the LCM 12: 8 numbers (12, 24, ..., 96). Union = 25 + 16 − 8 = 33, P = 0.33. Trap 0.41: forgetting to subtract the common numbers. Trap 0.37: using 4 × 6 = 24 for the common part (only 4 numbers); divisibility by both needs the LCM 12, not the product.

stat1-w6-q14.question: 3 people are chosen at random (without replacement) from 5 boys and 4 girls. What is the probability of exactly 2 girls?
stat1-w6-q14.explanation: Total ways = 9C3 = 84. Exactly 2 girls and 1 boy: 4C2 × 5C1 = 6 × 5 = 30. P = 30/84 = 5/14. Trap 1/14: forgetting the 5C1 for choosing the boy (6/84). Trap 80/243: the with-replacement calculation 3 × (4/9)² × (5/9). 10/21 = 40/84 is the probability of exactly 1 girl.

stat1-w6-q15.question: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability that the sum is at least 10 or both dice show the same number (a double)?
stat1-w6-q15.explanation: A = sum ≥ 10: (4,6), (6,4), (5,5), (5,6), (6,5), (6,6) = 6. B = double = 6. A ∩ B = (5,5), (6,6) = 2. P(A ∪ B) = (6 + 6 − 2)/36 = 10/36 = 5/18. Trap 1/3: forgetting to subtract the intersection (12/36). Trap 11/36: subtracting only one common outcome. 1/18 = 2/36 is just the intersection.

stat1-w7-q1.question: P(A ∩ B) = 0.12 and P(B) = 0.4. What is P(A | B)?
stat1-w7-q1.explanation: P(A | B) = P(A ∩ B) / P(B) = 0.12 / 0.4 = 0.3. Trap 0.048: multiplying instead of dividing (0.12 × 0.4).

stat1-w7-q2.question: A and B are independent events, P(A) = 0.5 and P(B) = 0.6. What is P(A ∩ B)?
stat1-w7-q2.explanation: For independent events, P(A ∩ B) = P(A) × P(B) = 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.3. Option 0 would apply if the events were mutually exclusive, not independent.

stat1-w7-q3.question: A fair die is thrown and you are told the number is even. What is the probability that the number is greater than 3?
stat1-w7-q3.explanation: Given even, the new sample space is {2, 4, 6}. Of these, greater than 3: {4, 6}. P = 2/3. Trap 1/2: ignoring the condition and writing P(X > 3) = 3/6.

stat1-w7-q4.question: A bag has 4 red and 6 blue balls. 2 balls are drawn without replacement. What is the probability that both are red?
stat1-w7-q4.explanation: P(first red) = 4/10, then 3 red and 9 in total remain: P(second red | first red) = 3/9. P = 4/10 × 3/9 = 12/90 = 2/15. Trap 4/25: assuming with replacement and computing (4/10)².

stat1-w7-q5.question: In a factory, Machine A makes 60% of the items, of which 2% are defective, and Machine B makes 40% of the items, of which 5% are defective. What is the probability that a random item is defective?
stat1-w7-q5.explanation: Total probability: P(D) = 0.6 × 0.02 + 0.4 × 0.05 = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. Trap 0.035: taking a simple average of 2% and 5%, when the machines' shares are different.

stat1-w7-q6.question: Machine A makes 60% of the items (2% defective) and Machine B makes 40% (5% defective). A random item turns out to be defective. What is the probability that it was made by Machine B?
stat1-w7-q6.explanation: P(D) = 0.012 + 0.020 = 0.032. Bayes: P(B | D) = 0.020 / 0.032 = 0.625. Trap 0.4: giving just B's production share; 0.375 = P(A | D).

stat1-w7-q7.question: P(A) = 0.4, P(B) = 0.5 and P(A ∩ B) = 0.2. What is correct about A and B?
options: They are complements of each other
stat1-w7-q7.explanation: P(A) × P(B) = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 = P(A ∩ B), so A and B are independent. Mutually exclusive would need P(A ∩ B) = 0, which is not the case. Complements would need P(A) + P(B) = 1 and intersection 0; here the sum is 0.9.

stat1-w7-q8.question: P(B) = 0.5 and P(A | B) = 0.6. What is P(A ∩ B)?
stat1-w7-q8.explanation: Multiplication rule: P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B) = 0.5 × 0.6 = 0.3. Trap 0.83: dividing 0.5 / 0.6. Trap 1.1: adding them, which cannot be a probability.

stat1-w7-q9.question: Of 100 students, 40 took Maths, 30 took Stats and 10 took both. It is known that a random student took Maths. What is the probability that the student also took Stats?
stat1-w7-q9.explanation: P(Stats | Maths) = P(both) / P(Maths) = 10/40 = 0.25. After the condition, the sample space is only the 40 Maths students. Trap 0.1: 10/100 is the joint probability. Trap 0.33: 10/30 = P(Maths | Stats), the reversed condition.

stat1-w7-q10.question: Two students independently try to solve a problem. Their probabilities of solving it are 0.6 and 0.5. What is the probability that the problem gets solved (at least one solves it)?
stat1-w7-q10.explanation: Use the complement: both fail = 0.4 × 0.5 = 0.2 (multiply because of independence). P(at least one solves) = 1 − 0.2 = 0.8. Trap 0.3: this is the probability that both solve it. Trap 0.5: the probability that exactly one solves it (0.3 + 0.2). Trap 1.1: simply adding.

stat1-w7-q11.question: P(A) = 0.5, P(B) = 0.25 and P(A | B) = 0.8. What is P(B | A)?
stat1-w7-q11.explanation: First P(A ∩ B) = P(B) × P(A | B) = 0.25 × 0.8 = 0.2. Then P(B | A) = P(A ∩ B) / P(A) = 0.2 / 0.5 = 0.4. Trap 0.8: assuming P(A | B) and P(B | A) are the same. Trap 0.2: stopping at the intersection.

stat1-w7-q12.question: Bag 1 has 3 red and 2 blue balls, Bag 2 has 1 red and 4 blue. A bag is chosen by tossing a fair coin and one ball is drawn from it, which turns out to be red. What is the probability that the ball came from Bag 1?
stat1-w7-q12.explanation: Total probability: P(R) = 0.5 × 3/5 + 0.5 × 1/5 = 0.3 + 0.1 = 0.4. Bayes: P(Bag 1 | R) = 0.3 / 0.4 = 0.75. Trap 0.6: this is P(R | Bag 1), the reversed conditional. Trap 0.5: giving only the prior (the coin) and ignoring the information that the ball is red. 0.3 is the joint probability.

stat1-w7-q13.question: In an inbox, 30% of the emails are spam. The word 'offer' appears in 40% of spam emails and in 5% of normal emails. An email contains 'offer'. What is the probability that it is spam?
stat1-w7-q13.explanation: P(offer) = 0.3 × 0.4 + 0.7 × 0.05 = 0.12 + 0.035 = 0.155. Bayes: P(spam | offer) = 0.12 / 0.155 ≈ 0.774. Trap 0.4: taking P(offer | spam) as the answer. 0.12 is the joint probability and 0.155 is P(offer); both are unfinished steps.

stat1-w7-q14.question: A box has 5 good and 3 defective bulbs. 2 bulbs are drawn one after another without replacement. What is the probability that the second bulb is defective?
stat1-w7-q14.explanation: Total probability, conditioning on the first bulb: P = (5/8)(3/7) + (3/8)(2/7) = 15/56 + 6/56 = 21/56 = 3/8. This equals the probability for the first bulb, because without seeing the first bulb we get no new information. Trap 3/7: assuming the first bulb was good. Trap 2/7: assuming the first was defective. 3/28 is the probability that both are defective.

stat1-w7-q15.question: Two fair dice are rolled. A = 'the first die shows 4', B = 'the sum of the two numbers is 7'. Are A and B independent?
options: Yes, because P(A ∩ B) = 1/36 = P(A) × P(B)
No, because the sum depends on the number on the first die
No, because A and B are mutually exclusive
No, because P(B | A) = 1/36, which differs from P(B) = 1/6
stat1-w7-q15.explanation: P(A) = 6/36 = 1/6, and P(B) = 6/36 = 1/6 (6 ordered outcomes give sum 7). A ∩ B = only (4, 3), so P(A ∩ B) = 1/36 = 1/6 × 1/6: independent. Check: P(B | A) = (1/36) / (1/6) = 1/6 = P(B). For a sum of 7, every number on the first die works with exactly one number on the second, so knowing the first die does not change the probability of B. Trap: saying 'it depends' from intuition; independence is checked with the formula. Trap 1/36: mistaking P(A ∩ B) for P(B | A).

stat1-w8-q1.question: Which of these is a valid PMF?
stat1-w8-q1.explanation: In a valid PMF every value must be ≥ 0 and the sum must be 1. 0.2 + 0.8 = 1, correct. The first sums to 1.1, the second to 0.6, and the fourth has a negative probability.

stat1-w8-q2.question: Which of these is a discrete random variable?
options: Time spent waiting for a bus
Number of visitors to a website in a day
stat1-w8-q2.explanation: The number of visitors takes countable values like 0, 1, 2, ..., so it is discrete. Height, time and rainfall are measured and can take any value in between, so they are continuous.

stat1-w8-q3.question: PMF of X: P(X=1) = k, P(X=2) = 2k, P(X=3) = 3k, P(X=4) = 4k. What is the value of k?
stat1-w8-q3.explanation: The sum must be 1: k + 2k + 3k + 4k = 10k = 1, so k = 0.1. Trap 0.25: seeing 4 values and assuming 1/4, when the probabilities are not equal.

stat1-w8-q4.question: PMF of X: P(X=1) = 0.1, P(X=2) = 0.2, P(X=3) = 0.3, P(X=4) = 0.4. What is the CDF value F(2)?
stat1-w8-q4.explanation: F(2) = P(X ≤ 2) = P(X=1) + P(X=2) = 0.1 + 0.2 = 0.3. Trap 0.2: confusing the CDF with the PMF and writing only P(X = 2).

stat1-w8-q5.question: Two fair dice are thrown. X = the larger of the two numbers (maximum). What is P(X = 2)?
stat1-w8-q5.explanation: For max = 2, both numbers must be ≤ 2 and at least one must be 2: (1,2), (2,1), (2,2) = 3 outcomes. P = 3/36 = 1/12. Trap 2/36: forgetting (2,2).

stat1-w8-q6.question: CDF of a discrete RV X: F(x) = 0 (x < 0), 0.2 (0 ≤ x < 1), 0.5 (1 ≤ x < 2), 0.9 (2 ≤ x < 3), 1 (x ≥ 3). What is P(X = 2)?
stat1-w8-q6.explanation: P(X = 2) = the jump in the CDF at x = 2 = 0.9 − 0.5 = 0.4. Trap 0.9: taking F(2) itself as P(X = 2); 0.1 = P(X = 3).

stat1-w8-q7.question: X ~ Bernoulli(p = 0.7). What is P(X = 0)?
stat1-w8-q7.explanation: For a Bernoulli, P(X = 1) = p = 0.7 and P(X = 0) = 1 − p = 0.3. Trap 0.7: taking p as P(X = 0); p is always the probability of success (X = 1).

stat1-w8-q8.question: X is a discrete uniform random variable taking the values 1, 2, ..., 8. What is P(X = 5)?
stat1-w8-q8.explanation: In a discrete uniform, every value has probability 1/n = 1/8. Trap 5/8: this is P(X ≤ 5), the value of the CDF. Trap 1/5: putting the value 5 in the denominator.

stat1-w8-q9.question: A coin is tossed 3 times. X = the number of heads. Which values can X take?
stat1-w8-q9.explanation: The number of heads can be anything from 0 (TTT) to 3 (HHH), so the values of X are 0, 1, 2, 3. Trap '1, 2, 3': forgetting the case of 0 heads. Trap '1 to 8': taking the 8 outcomes of the sample space as the values of X; an RV gives each outcome a number, and many outcomes can get the same number.

stat1-w8-q10.question: X takes the values 1, 2, 3, 4 and its CDF is: F(1) = 0.15, F(2) = 0.40, F(3) = 0.75, F(4) = 1. What is P(1 < X ≤ 3)?
stat1-w8-q10.explanation: P(1 < X ≤ 3) = F(3) − F(1) = 0.75 − 0.15 = 0.60, i.e. P(X = 2) + P(X = 3) = 0.25 + 0.35. Trap 0.75: this is P(X ≤ 3), which also includes X = 1. Trap 0.35: taking only P(X = 3). 0.85 is P(X > 1).

stat1-w8-q11.question: Two fair dice are rolled. X = the sum of the two numbers. What is P(X ≤ 4)?
stat1-w8-q11.explanation: X = 2: (1,1) → 1 outcome; X = 3: (1,2), (2,1) → 2; X = 4: (1,3), (2,2), (3,1) → 3. Total 6 outcomes, P = 6/36 = 1/6. Trap 1/12: taking only P(X = 4) = 3/36. Trap 3/11: treating the 11 possible sums as equally likely. Trap 5/36: forgetting (2,2).

stat1-w8-q12.question: A bag has 3 red and 2 blue balls. 2 balls are drawn without replacement. X = the number of red balls drawn. What is the value of the CDF F(1)?

stat1-w8-q13.question: The PMF of X is P(X = x) = k·x², where x = 1, 2, 3. What is P(X ≥ 2)?

stat1-w8-q14.question: The CDF of a discrete RV X: F(x) = 0 (x < 1), 0.3 (1 ≤ x < 3), 0.5 (3 ≤ x < 5), 1 (x ≥ 5). What are P(X > 2) and P(X = 4)?
stat1-w8-q14.explanation: P(X > 2) = 1 − F(2) = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7. The CDF jumps only at x = 1, 3, 5, so X takes only the values 1, 3, 5; there is no jump at x = 4, so P(X = 4) = 0. Trap 0.5 (for P(X = 4)): taking the jump at x = 5 (1 − 0.5) as P(X = 4). Trap 0.5 (for P(X > 2)): using 1 − F(3) instead of 1 − F(2).

stat1-w8-q15.question: A fair die is rolled 2 times. X = the number of sixes obtained. What is P(X = 1)?
stat1-w8-q15.explanation: For X = 1, either a six comes first and not second (1/6 × 5/6), or the other way round (5/6 × 1/6). P = 2 × 5/36 = 10/36 = 5/18. Trap 5/36: counting only one order. Trap 11/36: this is P(X ≥ 1), which also includes (6, 6). Trap 25/36: this is P(X = 0).

stat1-w9-q1.question: What is the expected value E[X] of the outcome X of a fair die?
stat1-w9-q1.explanation: E[X] = (1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6) / 6 = 21 / 6 = 3.5. The expected value need not be a possible outcome. 21 is just the sum.

stat1-w9-q2.question: E[X] = 4. What is E[3X − 2]?
stat1-w9-q2.explanation: By linearity, E[3X − 2] = 3 × 4 − 2 = 10. Trap 14: reading the minus as a plus (3 × 4 + 2), and 12 = forgetting the constant.

stat1-w9-q3.question: Var(X) = 4. What is Var(−2X + 5)?
stat1-w9-q3.explanation: Var(aX + b) = a² Var(X) = (−2)² × 4 = 16. The constant 5 has no effect. Trap −8: not squaring a; variance is never negative.

stat1-w9-q4.question: X takes values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.2. What is Var(X)?

stat1-w9-q5.question: In a game you pay ₹10 and throw a fair die. If a six comes up you get ₹30, otherwise nothing. What is the expected net gain in one game?
stat1-w9-q5.explanation: Expected winning = 30 × 1/6 = ₹5. The entry fee is ₹10, so net = 5 − 10 = −₹5. In the long run, you lose ₹5 per game on average. Trap ₹5: forgetting to subtract the fee.

stat1-w9-q6.question: X and Y are independent, Var(X) = 3 and Var(Y) = 5. What is Var(2X − Y)?
stat1-w9-q6.explanation: Var(2X − Y) = 2² Var(X) + (−1)² Var(Y) = 4 × 3 + 5 = 17. Trap 7: subtracting Y's variance (12 − 5); trap 11: not squaring the 2 (6 + 5).

stat1-w9-q7.question: X takes the values 0, 2, 5 with probabilities 0.5, 0.3, 0.2. What is E[X]?
stat1-w9-q7.explanation: E[X] = 0 × 0.5 + 2 × 0.3 + 5 × 0.2 = 0 + 0.6 + 1.0 = 1.6. Trap 2.33: taking the simple average of the values (7/3) and ignoring the probabilities. 7 is just the sum of the values, and 0.6 is only the middle term (2 × 0.3).

stat1-w9-q8.question: Var(X) = 9. What is SD(2X + 1)?
stat1-w9-q8.explanation: SD(X) = √9 = 3. SD(aX + b) = |a| × SD(X) = 2 × 3 = 6; the constant 1 has no effect. Trap 36: this is Var(2X + 1) = 4 × 9. Trap 18: multiplying the variance by 2. Trap 7: adding 1 to the SD as well.

stat1-w9-q9.question: E[X] = 5 and E[Y] = 3. What is E[2X + Y]?
stat1-w9-q9.explanation: Linearity: E[2X + Y] = 2E[X] + E[Y] = 10 + 3 = 13. No independence is needed for this. Trap 16: applying the 2 to both (2 × 8). Trap 10: forgetting Y. 8 is E[X + Y].

stat1-w9-q10.question: In a game, the probability of winning ₹0 is 0.6, of ₹50 is 0.3 and of ₹200 is 0.1. What should the entry fee be for the game to be fair (expected net gain = 0)?
stat1-w9-q10.explanation: Expected winning = 0 × 0.6 + 50 × 0.3 + 200 × 0.1 = 0 + 15 + 20 = ₹35. In a fair game, fee = expected winning = ₹35, so that the net gain is 35 − 35 = 0. Trap ₹83.33: the simple average of the three prizes (250/3). Trap ₹250: the sum of the prizes. ₹50 is just the middle prize.

stat1-w9-q11.question: E[X] = 3 and E[X²] = 13. What is Var(2X − 4)?
stat1-w9-q11.explanation: Var(X) = E[X²] − (E[X])² = 13 − 9 = 4. Var(2X − 4) = 2² × 4 = 16; the −4 has no effect. Trap 4: stopping at Var(X). Trap 8: not squaring the 2. Trap 52: taking E[X²] as the variance and computing 4 × 13.

stat1-w9-q12.question: X takes the values 1, 2, 3 with probabilities a, 0.3, b, and E[X] = 2.2. What is Var(X)?

stat1-w9-q13.question: X = the outcome of a fair die, and Y = 1 if a fair coin shows a head, otherwise 0. X and Y are independent. What is Var(X + 2Y), approximately?
stat1-w9-q13.explanation: Die: E[X] = 3.5, E[X²] = 91/6 ≈ 15.17, so Var(X) = 91/6 − 12.25 = 35/12 ≈ 2.92. Coin: E[Y] = 0.5, E[Y²] = 0.5, so Var(Y) = 0.5 − 0.25 = 0.25. They are independent, so Var(X + 2Y) = Var(X) + 2² × Var(Y) = 2.92 + 1 = 3.92. Trap 3.42: not squaring the 2 (2 × 0.25). Trap 3.17: forgetting the factor 2 entirely. 2.92 is only Var(X).

stat1-w9-q14.question: The daily profit (₹) of a bike showroom is P = 200X − 500, where X = the number of bikes sold in a day. E[X] = 4 and Var(X) = 2.25. What are the expected value E and the standard deviation SD of the profit?
stat1-w9-q14.explanation: E[P] = 200 × 4 − 500 = 800 − 500 = ₹300. SD(X) = √2.25 = 1.5, so SD(P) = 200 × 1.5 = ₹300; the −500 has no effect on the SD. Trap SD = 450: multiplying the variance 2.25 by 200 instead of the SD. Trap SD = 90000: this is Var(P) = 200² × 2.25, not the SD. Trap E = 800: forgetting to subtract the fixed cost 500.

stat1-w9-q15.question: E[X] = 4 and SD(X) = 3. What is E[(X − 1)²]?
stat1-w9-q15.explanation: E[X²] = Var(X) + (E[X])² = 9 + 16 = 25. (X − 1)² = X² − 2X + 1, so by linearity E[(X − 1)²] = 25 − 2 × 4 + 1 = 18. Trap 9: taking (E[X] − 1)² = 3², i.e. moving E inside the square. Trap 25: finding only E[X²]. Trap 10: taking Var(X) + 1.

stat1-w10-q1.question: X ~ Binomial(n = 20, p = 0.3). What is E[X]?
stat1-w10-q1.explanation: Mean = np = 20 × 0.3 = 6. Trap 4.2: this is the variance, np(1 − p) = 20 × 0.3 × 0.7.

stat1-w10-q2.question: X ~ Poisson(λ = 4). What is Var(X)?
stat1-w10-q2.explanation: In a Poisson distribution, the mean and variance are both equal to λ, so Var(X) = 4. Trap 2: mistaking the standard deviation (√4) for the variance; 16 = λ² is wrong.

stat1-w10-q3.question: X ~ Binomial(n = 4, p = 0.5). What is P(X = 2)?
stat1-w10-q3.explanation: P(X = 2) = 4C2 × 0.5² × 0.5² = 6 × 1/16 = 6/16 = 3/8. Trap 1/16: forgetting the 4C2; trap 1/2: thinking '2 out of 4 is half'.

stat1-w10-q4.question: Calls arriving at a helpline each minute follow Poisson(λ = 2). What is the probability that no call at all arrives in a given minute? (e⁻² ≈ 0.135)

stat1-w10-q5.question: The probability of success on each attempt is 0.2 and attempts are independent. What is the probability that the first success comes exactly on the 3rd attempt?
stat1-w10-q5.explanation: Geometric: first two fail, then success = 0.8 × 0.8 × 0.2 = 0.128. Trap 0.488: this is 1 − 0.8³, i.e. 'a success at any point in the first 3 attempts'. Trap 0.032: swapping the success and failure probabilities (0.2² × 0.8).

stat1-w10-q6.question: A test has 5 MCQs, each with 4 options and one correct answer. A student guesses randomly on every question. What is the probability that at least one answer is correct?
stat1-w10-q6.explanation: X ~ Binomial(5, 1/4). P(none correct) = (3/4)⁵ = 243/1024. P(at least one) = 1 − 243/1024 = 781/1024 ≈ 0.763. Traps: 243/1024 is just 'none', and 405/1024 is 'exactly one' (5 × 1/4 × (3/4)⁴).

stat1-w10-q7.question: X ~ Binomial(n = 50, p = 0.2). What is Var(X)?
stat1-w10-q7.explanation: Var = np(1 − p) = 50 × 0.2 × 0.8 = 8. Trap 10: this is the mean np. Trap 0.16: forgetting to multiply by n (only p(1 − p)). Trap 40: taking only n(1 − p) and leaving out p.

stat1-w10-q8.question: The probability of success in each try is 0.25 and the tries are independent. What is the expected number of tries until the first success?
stat1-w10-q8.explanation: The mean of Geometric(p) = 1/p = 1/0.25 = 4. Trap 3: this is the expected number of failures before the success, but the question asks for tries (the successful try is also counted). Trap 0.25: taking p as the mean.

stat1-w10-q9.question: Which distribution is the most suitable to model the number of customers arriving at a shop in an hour (average 6 per hour)?
stat1-w10-q9.explanation: A count of events (customer arrivals) in a fixed time interval, with no fixed number of trials n, is modelled by a Poisson (λ = 6). A Binomial needs a fixed number n of trials. A Geometric counts the trial of the first success, and a Bernoulli is just one trial.

stat1-w10-q11.question: A Binomial random variable has mean 8 and variance 6. What are n and p?
stat1-w10-q11.explanation: np = 8 and np(1 − p) = 6. Divide: 1 − p = 6/8 = 0.75, so p = 0.25 and n = 8 / 0.25 = 32. Check: 32 × 0.25 = 8 and 32 × 0.25 × 0.75 = 6. Trap 'p = 0.75': taking 1 − p as p; then the mean would be 32 × 0.75 = 24, not 8.

stat1-w10-q12.question: A player's free throw succeeds with probability 0.8 each time (throws independent). What is the probability that at least 4 of 5 throws succeed?
stat1-w10-q12.explanation: X ~ Binomial(5, 0.8). P(X = 4) = 5C4 × 0.8⁴ × 0.2 = 5 × 0.4096 × 0.2 = 0.4096. P(X = 5) = 0.8⁵ = 0.32768. P(X ≥ 4) = 0.4096 + 0.32768 ≈ 0.737. Trap 0.410: taking only exactly 4. Trap 0.328: taking only exactly 5. 0.263 is P(X ≤ 3), the complement.

stat1-w10-q13.question: The number of errors on a website follows a Poisson distribution, with an average of 2 errors per hour. What is the probability of no error at all in a 30-minute period? (e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368, e⁻² ≈ 0.135)
stat1-w10-q13.explanation: 30 minutes = half an hour, so for this interval λ = 2 × 0.5 = 1. P(X = 0) = e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368. Trap 0.135: keeping λ = 2 and not scaling it to the time interval. Trap 0.632: this is the probability of at least one error (1 − e⁻¹). Trap 0.5: turning half an hour directly into the probability 0.5.

stat1-w10-q14.question: In a factory, each of 1000 items is defective with probability 0.002 (independently). Using the Poisson approximation, what is the probability of exactly 1 defective item? (e⁻² ≈ 0.1353)
stat1-w10-q14.explanation: n is large and p is small, so λ = np = 1000 × 0.002 = 2. P(X = 1) = e⁻² × 2¹ / 1! = 2 × 0.1353 ≈ 0.271. Trap 0.135: this is P(X = 0). Trap 0.406: this is P(X ≤ 1) = 3e⁻². 0.002 is just the probability that one item is defective.

stat1-w10-q15.question: A student clears an exam with probability 0.4 in each attempt (attempts independent). What is the probability that the first success comes on the 3rd attempt or later?
stat1-w10-q15.explanation: The first success coming on the 3rd attempt or later means the first 2 attempts both fail: 0.6 × 0.6 = 0.36. Trap 0.144: this is success exactly on the 3rd attempt (0.6² × 0.4). Trap 0.64: this is the probability of success within the first 2 attempts. Trap 0.216: 0.6³, the case of the 4th attempt or later.

stat1-w11-q1.question: X is a continuous random variable. What is P(X = 5)?
stat1-w11-q1.explanation: For a continuous RV, the area under a single point is zero, so P(X = 5) = 0. Trap f(5): the value of the density is not a probability. 0.5 is also wrong; there is no area at all under a single point.

stat1-w11-q2.question: X ~ Uniform(2, 10). What is the height of the PDF f(x) (for 2 ≤ x ≤ 10)?
stat1-w11-q2.explanation: f(x) = 1 / (b − a) = 1 / (10 − 2) = 1/8, so that the area of the rectangle is 8 × 1/8 = 1. Trap 1/10: dividing by the upper limit only.

stat1-w11-q3.question: X ~ Uniform(0, 12). What is P(3 < X < 7)?

stat1-w11-q4.question: A PDF is f(x) = c·x for 0 ≤ x ≤ 2, and 0 elsewhere. What is the value of the constant c?
stat1-w11-q4.explanation: The graph is a triangle: base 2, height f(2) = 2c. Area = ½ × 2 × 2c = 2c = 1, so c = 1/2. Trap 1/4: forgetting the ½ in the triangle area (2 × 2c = 4c = 1).

stat1-w11-q5.question: The waiting time for a customer to arrive is Exponential with mean 5 minutes. What is the probability that the wait is more than 5 minutes? (e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368)
stat1-w11-q5.explanation: The mean is 5, so λ = 1/5 = 0.2. P(X > 5) = e^(−0.2 × 5) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368. Trap 0.5: taking the mean as the median; the exponential is not symmetric. 0.632 = P(X ≤ 5).

stat1-w11-q6.question: A bulb's lifetime is Exponential with mean 1000 hours. The bulb has already run for 500 hours. What is the probability that it runs for another 1000 hours?
stat1-w11-q6.explanation: The exponential is memoryless: P(X > 1500 | X > 500) = P(X > 1000) = e^(−1000/1000) = e^(−1) ≈ 0.368. Trap e^(−1.5): this is P(X > 1500), which ignores the condition.

stat1-w11-q7.question: X ~ Uniform(4, 16). What is E[X]?
stat1-w11-q7.explanation: The mean of Uniform(a, b) = (a + b)/2 = (4 + 16)/2 = 10. Trap 8: taking just b/2. Trap 6: taking (b − a)/2, which is half the length of the interval, not the mean. 12 is just the length of the interval.

stat1-w11-q8.question: X ~ Exponential(λ = 0.25). What is the mean of X?
stat1-w11-q8.explanation: The mean of an Exponential = 1/λ = 1/0.25 = 4. Trap 0.25: taking λ itself as the mean. Trap 16: taking 1/λ². 0.75 = 1 − λ, which has no meaning here.

stat1-w11-q9.question: X is a continuous random variable and P(X ≤ 3) = 0.4. What is P(X < 3)?
options: f(3) is needed to find it
stat1-w11-q9.explanation: For a continuous RV, P(X = 3) = 0, so P(X < 3) = P(X ≤ 3) − P(X = 3) = 0.4. Trap 0.6: this is P(X > 3). f(3) is not needed, because the area under a single point is zero.

stat1-w11-q10.question: X ~ Uniform(2, 8). What is Var(X)?
stat1-w11-q10.explanation: Var = (b − a)²/12 = (8 − 2)²/12 = 36/12 = 3. Trap 36: forgetting to divide by 12. Trap 0.5: forgetting the square and taking 6/12. 5 is the mean, not the variance.

stat1-w11-q11.question: X ~ Exponential(λ = 0.5). What is P(2 < X < 4)? (e⁻¹ ≈ 0.368, e⁻² ≈ 0.135)

stat1-w11-q12.question: A PDF is f(x) = k(4 − x) for 0 ≤ x ≤ 4, and 0 elsewhere. What is P(X < 2)?
stat1-w11-q12.explanation: The graph is a triangle: base 4, height f(0) = 4k. Area = ½ × 4 × 4k = 8k = 1, so k = 1/8. From x = 2 to 4 there is a small triangle: base 2, height f(2) = 2/8 = 0.25, area = ½ × 2 × 0.25 = 0.25 = P(X > 2). So P(X < 2) = 1 − 0.25 = 0.75. Trap 0.5: taking half the area because 2 is the midpoint; the density is higher near x = 0. 0.25 is P(X > 2) and 0.125 is k.

stat1-w11-q13.question: X ~ Uniform(0, 10). It is given that X > 4. What is P(X > 7 | X > 4)?
stat1-w11-q13.explanation: P(X > 7 | X > 4) = P(X > 7 and X > 4) / P(X > 4) = P(X > 7) / P(X > 4), because X > 7 already implies X > 4. P(X > 7) = 3/10, P(X > 4) = 6/10, so the answer = 3/6 = 0.5. Trap 0.3: ignoring the condition and taking P(X > 7). 0.6 is P(X > 4) and 0.7 is P(X < 7).

stat1-w11-q14.question: The repair time of a machine is X ~ Exponential(λ = 0.2) (mean 5 hours). What is the time m for which P(X > m) = 0.5 (i.e. the median)? (ln 2 ≈ 0.6931)
stat1-w11-q14.explanation: P(X > m) = e^(−0.2m) = 0.5. Take ln of both sides: −0.2m = −ln 2, so m = 0.6931 / 0.2 = 3.4655 ≈ 3.47 hours. Trap 5: taking the mean as the median; the exponential is not symmetric, so its median is less than its mean. Trap 0.139: multiplying by λ instead of dividing (0.6931 × 0.2). 2.5 is just half the mean.

stat1-w11-q15.question: The CDF of a continuous RV X is F(x) = x²/9 for 0 ≤ x ≤ 3 (F = 0 for x < 0, and F = 1 for x > 3). What is P(1 < X < 2)?
stat1-w11-q15.explanation: P(1 < X < 2) = F(2) − F(1) = 4/9 − 1/9 = 3/9 = 1/3. Since X is continuous, < and ≤ make no difference. Trap 4/9: taking only F(2) = P(X ≤ 2). 5/9 = 1 − F(2) = P(X > 2), and 1/9 = F(1).

stat1-w12-q1.question: What is the relationship between the mean, median and mode in a normal distribution?
options: The mode is always the largest
stat1-w12-q1.explanation: The normal curve is perfectly symmetric around μ, so the peak (mode), the middle point (median) and the average (mean) all lie at μ. Mean > median > mode happens in right-skewed data.

stat1-w12-q2.question: According to the empirical rule, roughly what share of normal data lies between μ − 2σ and μ + 2σ?
stat1-w12-q2.explanation: 68-95-99.7 rule: 68% within ±1σ, 95% within ±2σ, 99.7% within ±3σ. So 95% for ±2σ.

stat1-w12-q3.question: Heights follow N(μ = 165 cm, σ = 5 cm). What is the z-score of a height of 177 cm?
stat1-w12-q3.explanation: z = (177 − 165) / 5 = 12 / 5 = 2.4. The height is above the mean, so z will be positive. Trap 12: forgetting to divide by σ.

stat1-w12-q4.question: X ~ N(μ = 50, σ = 8). Using the empirical rule, what is P(42 < X < 66) approximately?
stat1-w12-q4.explanation: 42 = μ − σ and 66 = μ + 2σ. From μ − σ to μ = 68% / 2 = 34%, and from μ to μ + 2σ = 95% / 2 = 47.5%. Total = 34 + 47.5 = 81.5%. Trap: taking just one side (68% or 95%).

stat1-w12-q5.question: Z is standard normal and Φ(1) = 0.8413. What is P(Z > −1)?
stat1-w12-q5.explanation: By symmetry, P(Z > −1) = P(Z < 1) = Φ(1) = 0.8413. Trap 0.1587: this is P(Z > 1); 0.6826 = P(−1 < Z < 1). A probability is never negative.

stat1-w12-q6.question: Marks follow N(μ = 70, σ = 10). The top 5% of students get an A grade. What is the minimum cutoff for an A grade? (Φ(1.645) = 0.95, Φ(1.96) = 0.975)
stat1-w12-q6.explanation: Top 5% means 95% of the area below the cutoff: Φ(z) = 0.95, so z = 1.645. Cutoff = 70 + 1.645 × 10 = 86.45. Trap 89.6: using 1.96, which is the cutoff for the top 2.5%. Trap 90: treating 2σ as 5%.

stat1-w12-q7.question: Marks follow N(μ = 80, σ = 6). What is the z-score of 71 marks?
stat1-w12-q7.explanation: z = (71 − 80) / 6 = −9 / 6 = −1.5. The value is below the mean, so z is negative. Trap 1.5: forgetting the sign. Trap −9: forgetting to divide by σ. −0.67 = 6 / (−9), using the formula upside down.

stat1-w12-q8.question: By the empirical rule, roughly what percent of normal data lies outside the range μ − σ to μ + σ?
stat1-w12-q8.explanation: About 68% lies inside μ ± σ, so 100 − 68 = 32% lies outside (16% on each side). Trap 68%: giving the inside part. Trap 16%: taking only one tail. 5% is the part outside ±2σ.

stat1-w12-q9.question: If X ~ N(μ, σ²), what are the mean and standard deviation of Z = (X − μ) / σ?
stat1-w12-q9.explanation: Subtracting μ makes the mean 0, and dividing by σ makes the SD σ/σ = 1. So Z ~ N(0, 1), the standard normal. Trap 'μ and σ': after standardizing, the original parameters do not remain. Trap '0 and σ': dividing by σ changes the SD too.

stat1-w12-q10.question: The weight of a fruit follows N(μ = 60 g, σ = 5 g). What is P(65 < X < 70)? (Φ(1) = 0.8413, Φ(2) = 0.9772)
stat1-w12-q10.explanation: z-values: (65 − 60)/5 = 1 and (70 − 60)/5 = 2. P = Φ(2) − Φ(1) = 0.9772 − 0.8413 = 0.1359. Trap 0.8185: taking Φ(2) − Φ(−1) = 0.9772 − 0.1587, as if the interval were on both sides of the mean. 0.9772 is only P(X < 70), and 0.1587 = P(X > 65).

stat1-w12-q11.question: X ~ N(μ = 20, σ = 3). What is the distribution of Y = 2X − 5?
stat1-w12-q11.explanation: A linear transform of a normal is also normal. Mean = 2 × 20 − 5 = 35, SD = |2| × 3 = 6. Trap 'SD 1': subtracting 5 from the SD too. Trap 'SD 36': writing the variance 2² × 9 = 36 as the SD. Trap 'mean 40': forgetting the −5.

stat1-w12-q12.question: Marks follow N(μ = 55, σ = 12). The bottom 10% of students get a remedial class. What is the cutoff (students below it go to the remedial class)? (Φ(1.28) = 0.90)
stat1-w12-q12.explanation: We need 10% of the area below the cutoff: Φ(z) = 0.10. By symmetry Φ(−1.28) = 1 − 0.90 = 0.10, so z = −1.28. Cutoff = 55 + (−1.28) × 12 = 55 − 15.36 = 39.64. Trap 70.36: taking z as positive (that is the top 10% cutoff). Trap 53.72: forgetting to multiply by σ (55 − 1.28). Trap 43: simply taking μ − σ.

stat1-w12-q13.question: X is normal with μ = 100, and P(X > 120) = 0.0228. What is σ? (Φ(2) = 0.9772)
stat1-w12-q13.explanation: P(X > 120) = 0.0228 ⇒ P(X ≤ 120) = 1 − 0.0228 = 0.9772 = Φ(2), so the z-score of 120 is 2. (120 − 100) / σ = 2 ⇒ σ = 20 / 2 = 10. Trap 20: forgetting to divide by z. Trap 40: multiplying by z instead of dividing. 0.1 = 2 / 20, the formula upside down.

stat1-w12-q14.question: Ravi scored 78 in Maths (class: μ = 70, σ = 4) and Sneha scored 85 in Stats (class: μ = 75, σ = 8). Marks in both classes are normal. Who is better relative to their own class, and roughly what percent of that student's classmates scored higher? (Φ(1.25) = 0.8944, Φ(2) = 0.9772)
stat1-w12-q14.explanation: Ravi: z = (78 − 70)/4 = 2. Sneha: z = (85 − 75)/8 = 1.25. Ravi's z is larger, so he is relatively better in his class. Above Ravi = P(Z > 2) = 1 − 0.9772 = 0.0228 = 2.28%. Trap Sneha: comparing raw marks (85 > 78) or the raw gap from the mean (10 > 8) while ignoring the SD. Trap 97.72%: giving the percent of students below Ravi. 10.56% is the percent of students above Sneha.

stat1-w12-q15.question: X ~ N(μ = 50, σ = 10). What is P(X < 35 or X > 65)? (Φ(1.5) = 0.9332)
stat1-w12-q15.explanation: z-values: (35 − 50)/10 = −1.5 and (65 − 50)/10 = 1.5. Each tail = 1 − 0.9332 = 0.0668, and by symmetry the two tails are equal: total = 2 × 0.0668 = 0.1336. Trap 0.0668: taking only one tail. Trap 0.8664: this is the middle part P(35 < X < 65). 0.9332 is P(X < 65).
